tier_reason: The repo page has no numbers. The claim comes from a peer-reviewed CIDR 2026 paper (Houlborg et al., 'Flexible I/O for Database Management Systems with xNVMe'), but vldb.org is egress-blocked, so it is known only from search snippets. That holds it at C until the paper is opened (a B candidate).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (CIDR 2026), per search snippet: DuckDB with the xNVMe-based nvmefs extension reaches comparable performance on non-I/O-intensive queries and up to 50% lower query times on I/O-intensive queries (aggregation, TPC-H) than DuckDB's default synchronous file I/O.
corrections.caveats: Paper PDF (vldb.org) is egress-blocked; claim taken from search snippets only. 'Up to 50% lower query time' is about 2x at best, not '50% faster', and it is measured at DuckDB level against DuckDB's default sync I/O, not as a raw I/O microbenchmark against io_uring/libaio. A related benchmark repo, itu-rad/nvmefs-benchmark (an ITU master's thesis on FDP write amplification), exists but carries no results, CPU model or flags on its page. There is also a companion arXiv paper, 'DuckDB on xNVMe' (2512.01490), which is blocked here. The repo README names the xnvmeperf tool but gives no numbers. The LICENSE file is BSD-3-Clause; the repo also has a LICENSES directory for other parts.

notes: This is a real, active Samsung-backed project. Retier to B if a session can open the CIDR paper and confirm the hardware and baselines. Last commit 2026-10-01; 318 stars.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine tables in the README against dust and pdu, with warm cache and 32 logical cores. No CPU model, no compiler flags and no published benchmark script, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux: ~/.cargo (57k files) 19.6 ms vs dust 202.2 ms (10.3x faster) but vs pdu -H 14.0 ms (1.40x slower); ~/programs (509k files) 143.8 ms vs dust 388.2 ms (2.7x) and pdu -H 228.3 ms (1.6x); /nix/store (1.2M files) 402.7 ms vs dust 1.118 s (2.8x) and pdu -H 1.401 s (3.5x). Windows 10/NTFS: 2.7-7.4x faster than dust and 2.0-6.2x faster than pdu (pdu without -H).
corrections.caveats: Brand-new, first-party, 0 stars. Warm page cache only; no CPU model, no published benchmark script. Loses to pdu on the smallest Linux tree. Its win over pdu on /nix/store comes from pdu's hard-link dedup scaling badly. The 3.5x figure is against pdu; against dust it is 2.8x.

notes: The record misattributed 3.5x to the dust comparison on /nix/store (it is 2.8x vs dust and 3.5x vs pdu); I added the dust 10.3x row and the Windows table. License MIT OR Apache-2.0 confirmed in Cargo.toml; last commit 2026-09-18.

tier_reason: The commit d2c31f4 ('linux: introduce io_uring support (#3952)') says only 'an 8x increase in throughput has been observed', with no workload, hardware or method. That is a directional claim, so it stays at D. The project is notable (27.2k stars).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Commit message (#3952): 'Performance looks great; an 8x increase in throughput has been observed.' No methodology given.
corrections.caveats: No workload, hardware or method is given; the baseline is libuv's own threadpool, not POSIX I/O. Per search results, libuv 1.49 made io_uring opt-in (UV_USE_IO_URING=1) after kernel and security problems (SQPOLL); in 1.50 io_uring is used for epoll batching, and the env var now affects only sqpoll. Default builds may therefore not use the io_uring file path at all. Node.js also patched io_uring off by default in its bundled libuv. Docs are CC-BY-4.0; code is MIT.
